newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - HK's housing plans bolster large developer.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK's housing plans bolster large developer.

text.p: Hong Kong's wealthy property developers hold the key to a government drive to boost housing supply, putting them in a strong position to reap the financial benefits, analysts say.
Housing is a top priority in this tiny territory, where a shortage of supply fuelled a 30 percent rise in property prices in the first half of the year.
The government has pledged to boost supply to an annual target of 85,000 units by 2001.
"It plays into the hands of the large land bank developers," said Michael Leary, senior property analyst at Lehman Brothers.
"At the end of the day Hong Kong needs housing and the developers have to provide most of it," he said.

While booming real estate prices have meant easy money for developers, the government is striving to moderate price growth and is counting on the private sector developers to produce 36,000 units of the total 85,000 target.
"Out of the 36,000 flats we earmarked for the private housing sector, we expect to put out new land to build 20,000.
"The balance of 16,000 is expected to come from private housing redevelopment. Now that depends a great deal on the private developers," Secretary for Housing Dominic Wong said.
"I am exhorting them to cooperate with the government," he told Reuters in an interview.
But since boosting supply is not in their interest, NAVA SC Securities research director Stephen Brown said developers would likely "extract a price which will again widen margins".
Property developers would be able to negotiate lower land premiums payable to the government to convert their existing land bank into land for residential use, he said.
"After you have got planning permission, you can sit there for up to two years and negotiate the premium."

"And if you don't like the premium you, can just walk away from the site. So the longer and longer you stretch it out, given the government need for supply, the cheaper and cheaper the premium is going to get," said Brown.
But Wong dismissed the idea of lower premiums.
"There is no reason why the government should go out of its way to subsidise the developers," he said.

Instead, developers would be encouraged to increase supply through other measures including the release of a five-year government land disposal programme, which boosts residential land supply by 140 percent compared with the prior five years.
Analysts said this also boosted the developers' positions.

"They actually know for the first time going forward the government's side of the supply equation. The guys who bid at the government land auction don't need to frenetically bid and their margins should widen somewhat," said Brown.
"Their business risk is going to fall as well because they are going to be able to look out two, three, four years."
But while the large property developers look like the winners in Hong Kong's new housing environment, the outlook is more challenging for the smaller developers, analysts said
"Slower price growth and higher supply imply that developers' earnings growth will rely more on volume growth rather than price escalation," ING Barings analyst Manfred Ho said in a recent report.
"Therefore, smaller developers with less financial muscle to increase (their) land bank may suffer from declining profit margins," he said.
Wong said the government was aiding small developers by releasing small plots of land at its land auctions.
But Brown said that offered little help.
"Small sites in Hong Kong, there is very little or no demand for them," he said.
"These buildings sell at a very different price from an integrated three million square feet development with school, shopping centres and everything else."

Meanwhile, even if the government achieves slower housing price growth in the future, lower premiums and vast agricultural land banks accumulated over the years at low prices will ensure sustained profit growth for major developers, analysts said.
"At least for the next three to four years you are going to see good growth, 15 to 20 percent, by the larger developers," said Leary.
"In the past, it has been very much price growth which has driven the earnings picture for the developers.
"Now volume is becoming key and that is going to be a critical aspect of sustaining growth which is what we are projecting for Sun Hung Kai Properties, Henderson Land and Cheung Kong," he said.
